opus-5.5.text:
I think the residual stream is one of the most useful mental models you can have for a transformer. The way I picture it, you've got this high-dimensional vector running straight through the network, from the embedding at the bottom to the unembedding at the top. Every layer, every attention head and every MLP, reads from that stream, does some computation, and then writes its result back by adding to it. Nothing overwrites anything; it's all additive.

So you can think of it a bit like a shared working memory, or almost a communication bus. Early in the network, a token's position in the stream mostly holds information about that token itself. As you move up, attention heads pull in information from other positions, and the MLPs do something closer to lookup, retrieving associations and facts, so the representation becomes richer and more contextual. By the end it's been shaped into something that can predict the next token.

One analogy I like is to compare it to how we think about the brain. You have this core stream, and different modules can each read off the pieces relevant to them and contribute their part. Because it's a sum, a later layer can pick up something written much earlier without the intermediate layers having to carry it forward deliberately. That's a big part of why these networks train well even when they're very deep. The gradients have a clean path, and each layer only has to learn an incremental update instead of re-deriving everything.

From an interpretability perspective, that additivity is a gift. You can ask what a given head contributed, decompose the final output into pieces from different components, and find circuits where one head writes something that another head several layers later reads. That's how people found things like induction heads.

The complication is superposition. The stream has a fixed width, maybe a few thousand to tens of thousands of dimensions, but the model wants to represent far more features than that. So it packs them in almost-orthogonal directions and tolerates a bit of interference, relying on most features being sparse and rarely active together. That's why you can't just look at individual neurons or dimensions and read off clean concepts, and why techniques like sparse autoencoders, which try to pull out those underlying feature directions, have been so exciting.

So to sum up: a shared, additive memory that every component reads from and writes to, very crowded and heavily compressed, and one of the best handles we have on understanding what's actually going on inside these models.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes the residual stream as a “shared working memory.”

r002.rationale: It calls the stream a high-dimensional vector and says components read from it and write to it, but does not state that computations operate on subspaces of that vector.

r003.rationale: It explains that the stream has limited width and packs far more features into almost-orthogonal directions, identifying this as superposition.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is the residual stream is basically the model's working memory, or like its scratchpad, that it carries along as it processes each token. Every layer reads from it and writes back into it, and the key thing is that it's additive. A layer doesn't overwrite what came before, it just adds a vector on top. So the stream at the end is really a sum of everything every attention head and every MLP decided to contribute along the way.

I find that framing really useful because it means you can think of the layers as a bunch of relatively independent components all communicating through this shared channel, rather than a strict pipeline where layer five only matters because of what layer four handed it. An attention head early on can write something that an MLP ten layers later reads directly. It's more like a bus than a chain.

The other thing that falls out of it is this idea of superposition and bandwidth. The residual stream has a fixed width, say a few thousand dimensions, but the model wants to track way more features than that. So it ends up packing features into directions that aren't orthogonal, and different components have to be careful about which subspaces they read and write to so they don't clobber each other. A lot of the interpretability work, like what the Anthropic team has done with sparse autoencoders, is really about trying to unpack that compressed representation back into human-legible features.

And then from a scaling perspective, I think it's one of the reasons transformers are so nice to train. Because of the additive structure, gradients flow straight through, which is the classic ResNet insight, and it means you can keep stacking depth without the optimization falling apart. So you get this architecture that's simultaneously easy to optimize and surprisingly natural to reason about as a communication substrate between components. That combination is a big part of why it's held up as well as it has.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes the residual stream as the model’s “working memory” or “scratchpad.”

r002.rationale: It says components read from and write to the residual stream’s subspaces, after noting its fixed width of a few thousand dimensions.

r003.rationale: It explains that the model tracks more features than the stream has dimensions by packing features into non-orthogonal directions, describing superposition in a single vector.

astra-6.text:
I think of the residual stream as a shared workspace that all the layers can read from and write to. You start with a vector at each token position, and then each attention block and MLP adds something to that vector. So the computation is this accumulation of updates, rather than each layer completely replacing the representation from the previous one.

Attention lets a position pull in information from other positions, while the MLP does computation on the information available at that position. And because there’s this additive path through the network, information can persist until a later layer needs it.

The thing that makes this picture a little tricky is that the vector isn’t a neat list of variables where one coordinate means “this is a noun” and another means “we’re talking about France.” Features can be represented by directions, and those representations can overlap. So “shared workspace” is a useful intuition, but it’s a workspace with a learned encoding, rather than a set of human-readable slots.

r001.rationale: It describes the residual stream as a shared workspace that layers read from and write to, with information persisting for later layers—clearly conveying working memory.

r002.rationale: It says features can be represented by overlapping directions, but does not state that computations operate on subspaces of the high-dimensional residual vector.

r003.rationale: It mentions overlapping feature representations, but does not clearly explain that many distinct feature vectors are packed into one vector through superposition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the residual stream as a shared communication channel between all the different parts of the model. You have this vector at each token position, and each attention head or MLP gets to read from it and then write an update back into it.

The useful distinction is between the residual stream and the computation happening around it. An attention head can move information between token positions, while an MLP can compute something using the information available at a particular position. They put their results back into this common space, where later layers can use them.

And that space doesn’t necessarily have one dimension for each concept. Features can be represented as directions, and you can fit many more features into the space than you have dimensions, provided they’re sufficiently sparse. So I wouldn’t picture it as a neat collection of named registers. It’s more like a shared workspace with lots of overlapping representations, which the model learns to read and modify.

r001.rationale: It describes the residual stream as a shared workspace that components read and update and later layers use, conveying the model’s working memory.

r002.rationale: It describes components reading the residual vector and features as directions, but does not state that computations operate on subspaces of that vector.

r003.rationale: It says many more features than dimensions can be represented in the shared space through sparse, overlapping representations, conveying superposition.
